keyboard_models:
I built both keyboards as static MuJoCo geoms on a desk plane (desk friction 0.6), in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-tualyn/088f8e83-392a-5b19-ac2c-5c0005fbdef6/scratchpad/klavye/sesame/kbterrain.py. Every keyboard surface has contact priority 1, so the test friction (0.3, 0.4 or 0.6) is what applies under every foot.

**K1 (laptop / chiclet keyboard)**
- Laptop base: one box, deck height 8-12 mm (random per trial).
- Keycaps: box caps, 15-16 mm square for a 1u key, on a 19 mm pitch, so gaps are 3-4 mm.
- Caps stand 1.5-2.0 mm above the deck.
- Layout: ANSI main block with a 6.25u space bar and a half-depth F row.
- For the along-rows test it is the real depth: 90 mm palm rest in front, a 15 mm hinge strip behind, then the open lid as a wall leaning back 20°. The layout is repeated twice lengthwise so a 25 cm path stays on keys.
- For the diagonal test the layout is repeated 2 wide x 4 deep.

**K2 (full-size mechanical keyboard)**
- Plate: one continuous tilted plane, 20-30 mm above the desk at the front, tilted 4-6° (higher at the back). The case rim (10 mm) is at plate height.
- Keycaps: tapered frustum meshes. The base is 18 mm wide, 2 mm above the plate, with a switch housing underneath. The tops are 7-10 mm above the plate, with 5-6 mm gaps (1u tops about 13-14 mm) on a 19.05 mm pitch.
- Sculpted rows: the home row is lowest, with 0-2 mm steps between rows.
- Full ANSI-104 layout: 6.25u space bar, 2u numpad keys, the 0.5u trench in front of the F row, 0.25u trenches between the main, navigation and numpad blocks, and the empty navigation-cluster positions, which are open pits down to the plate.
- Along rows uses one real board (428 x 124 mm key field). Diagonals use the layout repeated 4 deep on the same continuous tilted plate.

**Robot model**
- Stock Sesame from the sesame-ml MJCF, with mesh-hull body collisions (the sesame_plus build): Enclosed cover, 384 g.
- 8 servos modelled as MG90S: position control kp 5, 0.20 N·m stall, 11 rad/s no-load speed with the torque-speed limit, 600°/s slew.
- Feet: 7 mm spheres. The real tips are about 12.8 mm round, so they cannot drop into 5-6 mm cap gaps. Only the F-row trench, the navigation pits and the gap after Esc can catch a foot.
- One correction to the model: the sesame-ml base centre of mass sits 4.75 mm to one side of the leg footprint, so I moved it to the footprint centre to match the symmetric frame. With the original offset the crawl drifts sideways about 100 mm per 25 cm.

**Test protocol**
- The robot starts already standing on the keys.
- 10 random starts per cell (seeds 1-10): random position within one key pitch, ±5° yaw, and every keyboard dimension randomised within the ranges above.
- Headings: along the rows, and 45° diagonal (on K2 both uphill and downhill).
- Success: covers 250 mm along the commanded heading within 30 s, with all of these true the whole time:
  - no fall (tilt over 45°);
  - not off the keyboard (two feet or the body on the desk, or the footprint centre off the board);
  - no foot stuck (a foot moving less than 4 mm in 3 s);
  - no stall (less than 10 mm progress in 6 s);
  - heading error under 60°.
baseline_result:
**Stock firmware gait (runWalkPose, real timing: 100 ms per frame, 20 ms between servo writes), open loop: 38/150 keyboard runs.**

- K1 along rows: 9/30, at 3.1-3.5 cm/s.
- K1 diagonal: 17/30.
- K2 along rows: 0/30.
- K2 diagonal uphill: 1/30.
- K2 diagonal downhill: 11/30.
- Even flat desk: 12/30.

The main failure is heading drift. The asymmetric gait turns a median 36-60° per 25 cm and lurches 25-45 mm backward in its start frame. Its rear feet lift only 2-3 mm; the front feet lift about 20 mm.

**Firmware gait plus steering: 71/150.** This uses the firmware's own turn sequences, inserted whenever heading error exceeds 35° (it stands in for a person pressing the web-UI arrows, or an IMU).
- K1 along rows: 24/30.
- K1 diagonal: 23/30.
- K2 along rows: 1/30.
- K2 diagonal uphill: 2/30.
- K2 diagonal downhill: 21/30.
- Speed drops to 2.3-3.9 cm/s.

**Climbing from the desk with the firmware gait: 0/24 on K1 and 0/24 on K2**, open loop or steered. The front feet get onto the laptop deck, but the rear feet keep hitting its 8-12 mm edge.
best_gait:
**Tuned higher-step crawl.** This is a firmware-only change on stock hardware. I tuned it with CEM on separate training seeds (1000 and up), then evaluated on seeds 1-10.

**Gait pattern**
- One leg in the air at a time, in the order left-rear, left-front, right-rear, right-front.
- All four feet are down about 79% of the time.
- Swing: the knee lifts first, then the hip moves, then the knee lowers.
- Body sway: the robot shifts its body sideways away from the lifting leg, using the front and rear hips in opposite directions.

**Parameters** (saved in out/crawl_params.json)
- Cycle period: 0.94 s.
- Hip stride: ±21.6°.
- Knee lift in swing: 61.6°, which gives 13-17 mm real foot clearance on all four feet (firmware gives about 20 mm front and 2-3 mm rear).
- Swing ramp: 0.27; hip movement delay within the swing: 0.46.
- Front hips turned 7° back, rear hips turned 3° forward.
- Knees lowered 10° in stance.
- Body sway: 18.8° with phase 0.30 (shifts the body away from the lifting leg).
- Turn trim: about 0.

**Results**
- Keyboard total: 97/150, against 38 for the stock firmware gait.
- K1 along rows: 29/30. K1 diagonal: 29/30.
- K2 downhill diagonal: 28/30. K2 uphill diagonal: 11/30.
- Speed is 5.7-7.9 cm/s on successful runs. Treat these speeds as optimistic: both this gait and the firmware gait slide each foot about as far as the body travels, because hip-yaw spider legs can't plant without scrubbing. With body sway off, the same crawl does 2.6-3.0 cm/s.

**IMU heading-hold variant** (adds an MPU6500; parameters in out/crawl_imu_params.json): 96/150, no better overall. It helps the K2 uphill diagonal (18/30 against 11/30) and loses a few runs elsewhere, which is within the noise.

**Dedicated K2 along-rows "keyboard mode"**: a separate tuning run (10 generations of 20 candidates x 9 trials) with the stance free to narrow by up to 40° found 0 successes.

Speeds are the median of the successful runs.

**How each gait fails**
- Stock firmware gait: mostly turning away (heading error over 60°).
- K2 along rows, every gait: stepping off the front or back edge of the case within about 1.3 s. Sesame's footprint is 116 x 107 mm and the board is 124 mm deep. The swing foot also moves 20-50 mm outward when the knee lifts. Standing still on the same start poses is stable.
- K2 uphill diagonal with the crawl: a mix of turning away, falls and stepping off the board.

**Climbing onto the keyboard from the desk** (8 tries per friction, head-on approach; success = footprint centre over the keys, nothing touching the desk for 1 s, tilt under 30°)

|---|---|---|---|
| K1 laptop (8-12 mm deck edge) | 0/24 | 11/24 (3.5-4.4 s when it works) | 13/24 |
| K2 mechanical (20-30 mm case + 7-10 mm caps) | 0/24 | 0/24 | 0/24 |
verdict:
**Stock Sesame cannot walk on a keyboard with its own firmware gait.** It managed 38 of 150 keyboard runs in simulation, and even on a flat desk it turns more than 60° within 25 cm at friction 0.6. The keys themselves are not the main problem: its ~13 mm round foot tips simply ride over the 3-6 mm gaps between keycaps. The real problems are heading drift, an asymmetric start lurch, and rear feet that lift only 2-3 mm.

**A tuned higher-step crawl fixes the laptop/chiclet keyboard.** This is a firmware-only change, so it adds no hardware and no soldering. It succeeded in 58 of 60 runs on K1 (along the rows and diagonally) at all three keycap frictions, and it climbs onto a laptop from the desk about half the time.

**The full-size mechanical keyboard stays hard.**
- Diagonal walking works downhill (28/30) but only partly uphill (11/30; 18/30 with an IMU).
- Walking along the rows of a real board failed every time (0/30) with every gait, including a dedicated narrow-stance search. Sesame is as wide as the board is deep, so a foot steps off the case almost immediately.
- Climbing onto it from the desk also failed every time (0/24), because the 27-40 mm step is about as tall as Sesame's 30 mm belly clearance.

**Comparison with Tarçın.** The sibling agent's preliminary Tarçın baseline (klavye/tarcin/out/batch_baseline.json, written at 14:16, 8 starts per cell) shows K1 48/48, K2 diagonal 13/24 and K2 along rows 0/24 ("fell"). So on keyboards a tuned-crawl Sesame is in the same class as Tarçın: both handle laptop keyboards and both fail along the rows of a full-size mechanical board. That baseline may have changed since, so check its final numbers before deciding.

**Caveats**
- These are simulation results only, so treat speeds as optimistic. Both gaits move by sliding the feet, so real speeds may be noticeably lower.
- The tuned crawl runs the hips harder: about 80% of stall at the 95th percentile, against about 50% for the stock firmware gait. It held up with 0.16 N·m servos and with +15% mass, but expect warmer hip servos and more wear.
- I moved the model's centre of mass onto the leg footprint centre (see the keyboard_models section). That matters for the crawl's sideways drift.
servo_loads:
Measured on the keyboard cells (not the flat desk). MG90S is modelled at 0.20 N·m stall with an 11 rad/s torque-speed limit. "At limit" means the share of time a servo sits on that torque-speed limit while carrying at least 0.05 N·m.

| gait | knee p95 (N·m) | hip p95 (N·m) | knee at limit | hip at limit | peak |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stock firmware gait | 0.107 (cells 0.08-0.14) | about 0.10 | 7.6% | 8.4% | 0.20 on brief impacts |
| Firmware + steering | 0.103 | 0.094 | 6.6% | 6.8% | 0.20 |
| Tuned crawl | 0.090-0.118 | 0.156-0.169 (78-85% of stall) | 7.8% | 15.7% | 0.20 |
| Crawl + IMU | 0.094 | 0.158 | 6.6% | 14.6% | 0.20 |

The 99th percentile reaches 0.20 N·m on most K2 cells, from impacts and slips.

**Sensitivity of the tuned crawl at friction 0.4** (10 runs per cell; columns K1 rows / K1 diagonal / K2 uphill / K2 downhill):

| servo stall, mass | K1 rows | K1 diag | K2 uphill | K2 downhill | knee p95 | hip p95 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.20 N·m, 384 g | 9 | 10 | 6 | 10 | 0.099 | 0.158 |
| 0.16 N·m, 384 g | 10 | 10 | 10 | 10 | 0.092 | 0.140 |
| 0.20 N·m, +15% | 10 | 8 | 5 | 8 | 0.107 | 0.159 |
| 0.16 N·m, +15% | 10 | 10 | 7 | 9 | 0.098 | 0.142 |

Weaker servos or a heavier robot did not make it worse. Torque margin is not what limits keyboard walking; the limits are footprint width against keyboard depth, and heading and lateral drift. The hips do run close to stall, so expect heat and wear.
climb_onto_keyboard:
The robot starts on the desk and approaches the keyboard's front edge head-on: front feet 15-25 mm from the edge, ±20 mm sideways offset, ±5° yaw, 30 s limit, 8 tries per friction. Success means the footprint centre is over the key field (at least one row in), nothing on the robot touches the desk for 1 s, and tilt is under 30°.

**K1, laptop (8-12 mm deck edge, palm rest, keys, lid behind)**
- Stock firmware gait: 0/24 open loop, 0/24 steered. The front feet get onto the deck, but the rear feet lift only 2-3 mm and keep hitting the edge.
- Tuned crawl: 11/24 (friction 0.3/0.4/0.6: 3/5/3). When it works it takes 3.5-4.4 s.
- Crawl + IMU: 13/24 (4/3/6).
- When a climb fails, the robot pivots on a rear foot caught at the deck edge, slides back off, and the open-loop gait then wanders away.

**K2, mechanical (case front 20-30 mm plus caps 7-10 mm, so a 27-40 mm step)**
- 0/24 with every gait, mostly falls (11-14 per crawl variant) and timeouts.
- The step is about as tall as Sesame's 30 mm belly clearance. The front feet can reach about 38 mm only with the knee at 90°, which leaves the rear legs unable to lift the body.
